```{r Required_Libries}
library(tidyverse, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(readr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(tsibble, warn.conflicts = FALSE) #let's add the tsibble library
library(feasts, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(mixtime, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(ggtime, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
```

### The next step
Let's import the REQUIRED data sets into the project.
```{r dataSets_Import}
sl_energy <- read_csv("dataSource\\Energy_consump_SL.csv", skip = 1, show_col_types = TRUE)
lib_energy <- read_csv("dataSource\\Energy_consump_LIB.csv", skip = 1, show_col_types = TRUE)
gui_energy <- read_csv("dataSource\\Energy_consump_GUI.csv", skip = 1, show_col_types = TRUE)
```
### The next step
we now wrangle each data set into how we want it for a time series analysis.
We start with sl_energy dataset.
```{r Wrangle_and_Transform_Sierra_Leone_Energy_Data_Set}
#remove the first two columns
sl_energy <- sl_energy[, !(names(sl_energy) %in% c("API", "...2"))]
#slice the first row
sl_energy <- sl_energy |> slice(-1)
#transpose the df to matrix
sl_energy <- sl_energy |> t()
#trasform again to dataFrame
sl_energy <- as.data.frame(sl_energy)
#let's add a new index column
sl_energy <- sl_energy |> rowid_to_column(var = "index")
#lets rename our energy consumption observation column
sl_energy <- sl_energy |> rename(sl_en_cons = V1)
```
### Next with Liberia Dataset
```{r Wrangle_and_Transform_Liberia_Energy_Data_Se}
lib_energy <- lib_energy[, !(names(lib_energy) %in% c("API", "...2"))]
lib_energy <- lib_energy |> slice(-1)
lib_energy <- lib_energy |> t()
lib_energy <- lib_energy |> as.data.frame()
lib_energy <- lib_energy |> rowid_to_column(var = "index")
lib_energy <- lib_energy |> rename(lib_en_cons = V1)
```
### Next with the Guinea Dataset
```{r Wrangle_and_Transform_Guinea_Energy_Data_Se}
gui_energy <- gui_energy[, !(names(gui_energy) %in% c("API", "...2"))]
gui_energy <- gui_energy |> slice(-1)
gui_energy <- gui_energy |> t()
gui_energy <- gui_energy |> as.data.frame()
gui_energy <- gui_energy |> rowid_to_column(var = "index")
gui_energy <- gui_energy |> rename(gui_en_cons = V1)
```
#### Now let's create just one variable called data_years.
```{r get_the_yearTime_Data}
#lets load any data into it, i choose sl energy, you can choose anyone.
year_vals <- read_csv("dataSource\\Energy_consump_SL.csv", skip = 1, show_col_types = TRUE)
# let's remove the first cols
year_vals <- year_vals[, !(names(year_vals) %in% c("API", "...2"))]
year_vals <- year_vals |> slice(-1) #lets remove the empty row or the first row.
#let's pivot the table right with a pivot_longer fxb
year_vals <- year_vals |> pivot_longer(
    cols = names(year_vals),
    names_to = "years",
    values_to = "observations"
        )
# let's remove observation col and add an index col
year_vals <- year_vals[, !(names(year_vals) %in% c("observations"))] |> 
    rowid_to_column(var = "index")
year_vals <- year_vals |> as.data.frame() # convert your year_vals data to Data Frame again.
```
Our next step is to combine all tables into one using joins.
```{r Join_all_dataSets_into_one}
en_dset <- year_vals |> 
    left_join(sl_energy, by = "index") |> 
    left_join(lib_energy, by = "index") |> 
    left_join(gui_energy, by = "index") |> 
    as.data.frame() # don't forger to convert your new table to dataFrame.
```
Let's clean our space
```{r Lets_keep_our_space_tidy }
rm("gui_energy", "lib_energy", "sl_energy", "year_vals") # removed stored variables
en_dset <- en_dset |> select(-index) #let's remove the index column
en_dset <- en_dset |> 
    mutate(date_year = as.integer(years), .before = 1) #let's modify the DF, add a new column and put as the first column in the DF
en_dset <- en_dset[, !(names(en_dset) %in% c("years"))]
```
#### Let's pivot our dataFrame
```{r We_do_our_final_Transformation}
# we use pivot longer
en_dset <- en_dset |>
    pivot_longer( #tihs to make the df longer and width shorter
        cols = c(sl_en_cons, lib_en_cons, gui_en_cons), # columns to pivot
        names_to = "country", # new column name of the pivoted column headers
        values_to = "energy_consumption" #new column name of the pivoted column values
    ) |>
    mutate(
        country = case_when( #we use this to match case and modigy the same country column
            country == "sl_en_cons" ~ "Sierra Leone", # if the value of a country is "sl_en_cons" change to "Sierra Leone"
            country == "lib_en_cons" ~ "Liberia", # if the value of a country is "lib_en_cons" change to "Liberia"
            country == "gui_en_cons" ~ "Guinea" # if the value of a country is "gui_en_cons" change to "Guinea"
        )
    )

```
### Let's enter the tides of TIME
```{r}
# let's turn the DataFrame to a tsbblie
en_dset <- en_dset |>
    as_tsibble(index = date_year, key = country) # let's convert to a time series table <tbl_ts>

```

#### *let's flex our muscle with some function building.*  😎

### let's create a function that can print out a trend chat when called upon.
```{r}
#let's create a variable called country_names with all the names of the countries in the table.
country_names <- en_dset$country |> unique()
#now let's create the function called country_trend.
country_trend <- function (val) {
    en_dset |> 
        filter(country == val) |> 
        autoplot(energy_consumption, aes(color = country)) +
        labs(
            title = sprintf("Trend Analysis of Net Energy Consumed in %s", val),
            subtitle = "Annual data from 1980 to 2024",
            x = "Year",
            caption = "This is an open source project. by Hassan S. Konneh 2026.",
            y = "Energy Consumed"
            # tag = "For Training Purposes"
            
        ) +
            theme_classic() +
            theme(
                plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
                plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "italic")
            )
}
# note, use sprintf(), and %s for text, %d for integers, %f for decimals, remember C++? 😎
```

#### Let's call the function "country_trend"
```{r}
country_trend("Sierra Leone") # Use any of the three countries
```

#### Let's add some smoothing curve to understand our trend
```{r}
country_smooth <- function (val) {
    country_trend(val) +
        geom_smooth( level = 0.95, span = 0.25) # level is the confidene band @ 0.95 as degault. Span control the curve smoothness.
}
```

#### Now let's call the new country_smooth function.
```{r}
#input the name of the country you want view with smooth trend
country_smooth("Sierra Leone")
```
